children.text: A useful blog introduction tells readers what the article answers and why they should continue. AI can draft options, but you must check their promises.
This guide focuses on writing and revising introductions with ChatGPT or another assistant, using clear briefs, examples, and an editorial checklist.
Start with the reader's question and the finished article
Write down the reader's task, their knowledge level, and the result your article can actually help them achieve.
Then review your outline or completed draft. An introduction should accurately represent the body, including important limitations.
You can draft an opening first or write it last. Revisit it after the article changes.

content.alt: Illustration suggesting writing the introduction after the main article

children.text: Writing the introduction last is one option. Revising an early draft after finishing the body also works.
Three useful ingredients, without a mandatory formula
Establish relevance
Name the specific problem or answer the main question. Avoid opening with a broad claim that could introduce any article.
Provide enough context
Explain what readers need to understand before the main steps. Technical tutorials may need a prerequisite or a warning about a common mistake.
Set accurate expectations
Describe the useful coverage that follows. Avoid promising rankings, conversions, or results your article cannot establish.

content.alt: Diagram of an introduction's purpose, relevance, and scope

children.text: Use these ingredients as editorial prompts, rather than a required search-engine structure.

content.alt: Diagram showing hook, bridge, and roadmap sections

children.text: Hook, bridge, and roadmap is one writing pattern. A direct answer may be more useful for a straightforward question.
Choose an opening pattern that fits the task
Direct answer
Illustrative example: 'A URL slug is the part of a page address that identifies its content. This guide shows how to draft one with AI.'
Use this when the reader needs a definition or quick instruction.
Problem and practical next step
Illustrative example: 'AI can produce a polished introduction that still promises too much. Start with the completed article and remove unsupported outcomes.'
Question and explanation
Illustrative example: 'Does every image need descriptive alt text? Its purpose determines whether a description, empty attribute, or longer explanation is appropriate.'
Answer the question promptly. Do not delay a simple answer merely to create suspense.
A real story or sourced fact
Use a short story only when it actually happened. Label invented scenarios as illustrative and never present fabricated results as your experience.
A statistic needs a credible source, date, and relevant population. If it does not help explain the article, omit it.

content.alt: Diagram showing several possible introduction patterns

children.text: Adapt the patterns to the article. Example wording and performance claims in older graphics are not verified results.
Prompt to draft introductions from a brief

content.code:
Draft three introductions for this article.
Reader and task: [brief]
Article title: [title]
Outline or completed draft: [content]
Verified facts and experience: [facts with sources, or none]
Create a direct-answer version, a problem-led version, and a concise explanatory version.
Name the topic early. Match the article's actual scope. Do not invent statistics, experience, testimonials, or ranking promises.
Avoid generic openings and unnecessary suspense. Explain any claim that needs checking.

children.text: Select the version that establishes relevance most clearly. Keep useful sentences from other versions only when they fit the same argument.

content.alt: ChatGPT interface showing introduction variations

children.text: These draft variations illustrate brainstorming. Their wording does not establish that a particular opening improves traffic.

content.alt: ChatGPT interface showing a drafted introduction

children.text: Check generated promises against the final article before publishing.
Prompt to improve an existing introduction

content.code:
Review this introduction against the article below.
Introduction: [text]
Article: [content]
Identify generic sentences, unsupported claims, missing context, and promises the article does not fulfil.
Suggest a revision that preserves the intended meaning and voice.
Keep necessary qualifications. Do not enforce a fixed word count, sentence limit, or keyword repetition rate.
List important changes and unresolved factual questions.

children.text: Compare the revised version with your original. AI may delete a caveat or introduce a new promise while making prose sound smoother.

content.alt: ChatGPT interface showing an introduction review checklist

children.text: An AI checklist is an editorial suggestion, rather than proof that the introduction meets Google's requirements.

content.alt: Illustration of drafting and refining a piece of content

children.text: Reviewing and refining a draft is part of the writing process.
Before-and-after examples
Remove a generic opening
Before: 'In today's fast-paced digital world, introductions are more important than ever.'
After: 'An AI-written introduction should explain the article's purpose without adding claims the body cannot support.'
The revision identifies the actual problem and avoids vague urgency.
Replace an unsupported promise
Before: 'These proven hooks will make your article rank and convert.'
After: 'These opening patterns give you ways to introduce a topic clearly. Choose one that fits your reader and article.'
Add an important prerequisite
Before: 'Use AI to change your published slug and improve SEO.'
After: 'Before changing a published slug, plan redirects and update internal links. This guide helps you decide whether a change is necessary.'
Length, keywords, and placement
There is no universal introduction length or first-100-words requirement. Use enough context without delaying the answer.
A short opening may suit a simple how-to question. A complex argument may require more setup.
Mention the subject naturally. Exact keywords do not need to appear within a fixed number of lines.
An H1, opening, and table of contents should work together for navigation. Their placement can vary with the layout and reader's task.
There is no documented universal crawl sequence from slug to metadata, schema, H1, and introduction.
Clear introductions can help readers understand a page. They do not automatically cause Google rankings or AI citations.

children.text: A meta description is a short HTML summary of a webpage. Google may use it in a search snippet, but can select page text instead.
Use AI to draft page-specific options, then check their accuracy, wording, and relevance. A useful description explains what the reader will actually find.
This guide covers length, examples, ChatGPT prompts, implementation, and common snippet problems.
I use AI while developing this content series for Do It With AI Tools. My goal is practical guidance with clear human review.
The examples below are illustrative. They are not measured CTR tests, recorded tool outputs, or promises of ranking improvements.
Draft options with the Meta Description Generator
What is a meta description
The description meta tag belongs in a page's HTML head. It normally does not appear as visible article text.

content.code:
<head>
  <meta name="description" content="Compare meta description examples and use AI prompts to draft an accurate summary for your page.">
</head>

children.text: The name attribute identifies the metadata. The content attribute holds your suggested summary.
A Google search snippet is the summary displayed with a result. It is not always the description you submitted.
Element
Purpose
Title tag
Suggests the page title; Google may select different title-link text.
Meta description
Suggests a page summary; it does not guarantee snippet wording.
H1 heading
Introduces the main topic visibly on the page.
Search snippet
Google's selected summary for a particular search.

content.alt: Search-result diagram labeling the title and description, with older length guidance corrected in the caption.

children.text: Correction to the older graphic: 150–160 characters and 900–950 pixels are not fixed Google limits. Actual snippet display varies.

content.alt: HTML diagram showing the description meta tag in the head section.

children.text: The description tag supplies a suggested page summary. It is not proof of a universal crawler or AI reading sequence.
Google's current guidance on search snippets
How long should a meta description be
Google sets no fixed maximum length for a meta description. Search snippets can be shortened to fit the available space, typically the device width.
Around 150–160 characters can be a convenient drafting target. It is not a requirement or a guarantee that the whole description will appear.
There is no separate fixed mobile limit either. Query, layout, selected text, and device width can change the result.
Write the main message early so the opening remains useful when the ending is missing. Do not force a keyword into a percentage-based position.
Keep the page topic and useful detail clear.
Remove repetition and filler before cutting important context.
Check the whole title-and-description combination.
Use desktop and mobile previews as approximations.
A short summary can work when it is informative. Do not add words merely to fill a meter or reach a minimum count.
Character and pixel counters can help editing. Their thresholds are tool settings, not universal Google display rules.

content.alt: Mangools preview diagram showing desktop and mobile snippet checks.

children.text: The graphic's pixel ranges and first-120-character exercise are optional editing aids. A simulator cannot reproduce every Google result.
Meta description examples for different pages
Choose details that distinguish the actual page. Use these examples as writing patterns rather than measured high-performing snippets.
Blog tutorials
Weak example: Learn everything about SEO and improve your results today.
Clearer example: Learn to write meta descriptions with AI prompts, page-specific examples, and review checks before publishing.
This version names the task and supporting material. It avoids promising rankings or a guaranteed increase in clicks.
Comparison articles
Example: Compare AI keyword research tools by features, access requirements, and limitations before choosing a workflow.
Say 'we tested' only when you actually tested the tools and explain the method on the page. Do not invent evaluation counts.
Product and tool pages
Example: Draft meta description options from your page summary, then review their clarity and accuracy before choosing one.
State 'free', 'no signup', or a usage limit only when the current offering supports the claim.
Product example: Explore the content planning template's sections, sample pages, and file format before downloading.
Service pages
Example: Explore SEO content writing for small businesses, including page planning, editing, and publishing support. Contact us to discuss your project.
This is a hypothetical service example. Include only the services and contact options your page actually offers.
Homepage and about pages
Homepage example: Do It With AI Tools offers AI guides, content creation workflows, SEO resources, and tools for creators and marketers.
About-page example: Meet Sufian Mustafa, founder of Do It With AI Tools, and learn about the platform's focus on AI, content creation, and SEO.
Use a broad site summary for the homepage. Explain the specific purpose of an about page instead of copying the same description.
Category and contact pages
Category example: Browse guides on writing titles, headings, introductions, and meta descriptions with AI prompts and human review.
Contact-page example: Contact Do It With AI Tools with questions about the website, resources, or collaboration opportunities.
Verify that the page provides the promised information. A description should summarize the destination, not advertise an unrelated offering.
How to write a useful meta description
Start with the page's purpose and the reader's task. Then describe a concrete reason the page may be useful.
Add detail beyond the title
Your title may already name the topic. Use the description to explain the method, audience, examples, or scope.
Some repeated topic wording is natural. There is no rule banning the same opening words as the title.

Match the reader's intention
A learner needs a tutorial. A tool-seeker needs a working generator. A buyer needs product details and a relevant next step.
Reader task
Useful description focus
Learn a process
Steps, examples, and what the guide explains.
Use a tool
Its purpose, inputs, and actual capabilities.
Compare options
Comparison scope and verified criteria.
Contact a business
Service scope and the available contact action.
Use direct answers for factual pages when they help. Do not withhold basic information merely to create curiosity.

Use natural wording and verified facts
Include topic terms when they fit. Exact-match wording, a single occurrence, and mandatory front-loading are not Google requirements.
Avoid a long keyword list. It tells readers less than a clear summary of the page.
Add dates, prices, authors, or product facts only when they are relevant and current.
Prefer specific details over generic claims such as 'unlock success' or 'boost results'. A factual summary can still be persuasive.

How to write meta descriptions with ChatGPT
Provide the actual page content or a reliable summary. A bare keyword leaves the assistant guessing about what the page delivers.
Page title and main heading.
Summary, intended reader, and content format.
Verified facts, features, and limitations.
Relevant topic terms and brand tone.
The action available on the destination page.
A prompt for five page-specific options

content.code:
Draft five distinct meta descriptions.
Title and H1: [paste]
Page content or reliable summary: [paste]
Reader and task: [describe]
Page type: [describe]
Verified facts and limitations: [list]
Available next action: [describe]
Topic terms and brand tone: [describe]

Describe only what this page provides.
Use natural English and add useful detail beyond the title.
Do not invent tests, prices, numbers, credentials, free access, or outcomes.
Avoid forced keyword positions and em dashes.
Keep each sentence within 25 words.
Aim for concise summaries; about 150–160 characters is an optional drafting target.
Do not pad shorter accurate options.
Explain each option's angle and flag uncertain claims.
Do not predict rankings, clicks, or AI citations.

children.text: Compare the options against the content rather than choosing the most confident wording. Check character counts with a counter instead of trusting AI arithmetic.

Rewrite it with a specific topic and useful page detail.
Offer one concise option and one fuller option.
Explain what you changed.

Why Google changes or ignores your meta description
Google primarily creates snippets from page content. It may use the description when that gives a more accurate summary for the search.
The same URL can therefore show different snippets for different queries. A rewrite is not automatically a mistake or penalty.
Your new description is not showing
Confirm that the correct live page contains the updated description tag.
Check for conflicting tags, a different canonical URL, or an old cached page.
Use Search Console URL Inspection to review Google's available information.
Request indexing after a meaningful update when appropriate.
Recrawling does not force Google to display your wording. There is no guaranteed update deadline.
Google shows navigation or unrelated page text
Check whether the main content clearly answers the query. Repeated boilerplate or unclear page copy may leave poor alternatives for a snippet.
Improve relevant text on the page as well as the description. Do not repeatedly rewrite metadata while leaving misleading content untouched.
An audit reports duplicate descriptions
First distinguish repeated text across URLs from multiple description tags on one URL. These are separate problems.
Repeated descriptions need page-specific wording where useful. Multiple tags may come from a theme, plugin, or template adding metadata twice.
Inspect the live HTML and fix the source of duplication. A different Google snippet does not prove that your HTML tag is duplicated.
The snippet is cut off
Move essential information earlier and remove filler. A preview can help, but cannot guarantee the exact layout or selected text.
Your page has no description
Google can still create a snippet from page content. Prioritize important pages when adding accurate descriptions instead of treating absence as an indexing block.

children.text: Review these as possible issues. A short description or preview overflow does not automatically reduce CTR or cause a penalty.

Use your CMS's SEO or search-listing field when available. After publishing, inspect the live HTML to confirm the field actually becomes a description tag.

Meta description versus Open Graph description
A description meta tag supplies a search summary suggestion. Open Graph descriptions supply metadata that social platforms can use in link previews.
They can share wording when it fits both contexts. Separate versions are useful when the audiences or preview purposes differ.
Meta description versus meta keywords
The description summarizes a page. The meta keywords tag is a separate field that Google does not use for web ranking.
Adding a keyword list there does not replace useful description writing.

Meta descriptions and AI search visibility
A useful page summary keeps metadata consistent with the content. It does not prove that an AI system will cite the page.
Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode use existing SEO fundamentals. They do not require special description wording or additional AI schema.
There is no published universal rule that every AI system treats the meta description as its first validation layer.
Keep useful answers and supporting evidence in visible page text. Metadata alone cannot compensate for inaccurate or incomplete content.

Review and measure your description updates
Choose a relevant page with enough search impressions to review. Check its queries, positions, countries, and devices before assuming low CTR is a copy problem.
Record the original description and update date.
Draft and review a page-specific replacement.
Publish it and verify the live description tag.
Compare query-level clicks, impressions, CTR, and positions over time.
CTR is clicks divided by impressions. Position changes, query mix, seasonality, and search-result features can affect it.
A before-and-after change is an observation, not a controlled A/B test. Google may also use different snippets from the submitted descriptions.
Do not promise a traffic lift or infer a ranking gain from a copy edit alone. Use the findings to guide your next revision.
